sections.heading: Chashma-i- Shahi
sections.content: Mughal Gardens were the Emperors' concept of paradise. These were developed as a retreat from their capitals during the summer. They were adorned with terraced lawns, gushing fountains, bright flowerbeds with the panorama of the lake in front of them - the three Mughal Gardens of Chashma-i- Shahi, Nishat and Shalimar. Shalimar Bagh, built by Emperor Jehangir for his wife Nur Jehan, is a beautiful garden with sweeping vistas over gardens and lakes, and shallow terraces. The plan of the garden is based on the Persian charbagh design in which a square garden is divided into four equal parts by water channels which are lined with polished stones. The garden has four terraces, rising one above the other. The lowest was the public garden while the middle one was the Emperors and the fourth terrace, by far the best, was reserved for royal ladies or the zenana. Nishat Bagh or the garden of bliss was designed in 1633 CE by Asaf Khan, brother of Nur Jehan during the reign of or the royal spring is a tastefully laid garden in terraces which was built by Shah Jehan. It is an exquisite garden laid around a natural spring.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Monument- Harvana Temple
sections.content: During the sixth century temples were erected in Kashmir by the Karkotaka Dynasty. These are characterized by lofty double pyramidal roofs and trefoiled doorways covered by triangular pyramidal pediments and columns. Facing either east or west, these temples get ample sunlight symbolizing dynamism and life. These temples have a cellular layout and have a pillared courtyard. Ancient stupas and chaityas in different parts of the region testify an early evidence of spread of Buddhism. The fifth century Harvana temple built with moulded terracotta tiles represents a wide range of themes including human forms, flora and fauna.

sections.heading: Ruins of Sun Temple, Martand
sections.content: Martand temple is dedicated to the Sun God. This eight century example of stone architecture reflects the influence of Gandhara style and local wooden prototypes conforming to the wooden model. The temple has steep sloping roofs.

sections.heading: Temple at Avantipur
sections.content: The famous Avantipur temples are believed to have been built in honour of lord Shiva by Avantivarman who is believed to have founded the city in the ninth century. The temples, although in ruins, are of great archaeological interest. There are two main temples, one larger and marked

sections.heading: Shankaracharaya Temple
sections.content: The temple of Shankaracharya occupies the top of the hill in the southeast of Srinagar where Shankaracharya stayed when he visited Kashmir in the ninth century from Kerala and delivered discourses. Built on a high octagonal plinth and approached by a flight of steps, it has sidewalls that once bore inscriptions and the main surviving shrine consists of a circular cell. A modern ceiling covers the inner sanctum and an inscription in Persian traces its origin to the reign of Emperor Shah Jehan. The original ceiling was dome- shaped and the brick roof is not more than a century old.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Monument- Jami Masjid
sections.content: Jami Masjid is in the heart of the old city of Srinagar, this is the largest mosque in Kashmir. Originally built by Sultan Sikandar in 1400, and extended by his son, Zain-ul- Abidin, it is a typical example of Indo-Saracenic architecture. It is built around a courtyard with 370 wooden pillars and galleries around it.The principal features of the mosque are the four minars and eight wooden columns as support and a tiered roof capped by a spire.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Monument- Alchi
sections.content: Ladakh has many historic monasteries called Gompas, where Buddhist Bhikkus (Bhikshus) and Bhikshunies have been living, studying and practicing their religion. Located in scenic locations the monasteries of Ladakh are, on hills and mountains and have rich collections of Buddhist Thangka paintings, art and artifacts. Alchi, a village in the Leh district is famous for one of the oldest monasteries in Ladakh, mainly known for its wall paintings of the eleventh century reflecting artistic and spiritual details of both Buddhism and Hindu kings of that time in Kashmir. The monastery was built by Lotsawa Rinchen Zangpo. At Alchi there are three shrines; the main one called Dukhang or Assembly Hall,the three-storeyed Sumtseg, and the Manjushri. There are also the votive stupas called the great Chörten and the small Chörten. Dukhang is the oldest monument preserved at Alchi. The entrance to the temple is through a courtyard and an elaborately carved doorway with panels of tiny Bodhisattvas and guardian figures. The hall has a niche at the back with a plaster image of Vairocana. The hall is painted with different mandalas. The entrance is flanked by an only partly preserved Life of the Buddha and a large depiction dedicated to donors and their the sides of the Alchi Photo Gallery niche is a depiction of attendant figures, feasts. Below the thousand Buddhas painted on animals and sacred symbols. Sumtseg, is dedicated to a triad of Bodhisattvas and their secondary deities located in three niches. The facade is carved in wood consisting of pillars, carved brackets, and capitals. Light penetrates through open shafts on each floor. The largest Bodhisattva on the back wall, Maitreya, is flanked by Avalokiteshvara and Manjushri. Besides these each niche has four secondary deities and two flying goddesses .Each of the Bodhisattvas are dressed in beautifully decorated garments. The Manjushri Temple is square with a large central platform. It supports the four pillars holding the diagonally arranged cross-beams of the ceiling. The four images of Manjushri are seated back to back in an elaborate common frame crowded various images of animals, gods and symbols and topped by the decorative scrolls deriving from the tails of the makaras. The Hemis Gompa is the biggest monastery in Ladakh.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: 1600-1650 Medieval Built in 1630 and houses monks of the Brokpa or Red Hat sect. Beautiful frescoes adorn the walls and the largest Thangka paintings in Ladakh can be seen here. The mask dance performed by the lamas at the Hemis monastery, during the Hemis festival is representative of the Mahayana Buddhist tradition of the victory of good over evil. Drums and long horns are the musical accompaniments. A thangka is a painted or embroidered Buddhist banner which was hung in a monastery or a family altar and occasionally carried by monks in ceremonial processions. Thangka, has different functions. Images of deities can be used as teaching tools when depicting the life (or lives) of the Buddha, describing historical events concerning important Lamas, or retelling myths associated with other deities. Devotional images act as the centerpiece during a ritual or ceremony and are often used as mediums through which one can offer prayers or make requests. Overall, and perhaps most importantly, religious art is used as a meditation tool to help bring one further down the path to enlightenment. Painted thangkas are done on cotton canvas or silk with water soluble pigments, both mineral and organic, tempered with a herb and glue solution. The entire process demands great mastery over the drawing and perfect understanding of iconography. The composition of a thangka, is highly geometric. Arms, legs, eyes, nostrils, ears, are all in a systematic grid of angles and intersecting lines.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Monument- Thicksey Monastery
sections.content: One of the finest examples of architecture from Ladakh, Thicksey Monastery is one of the most important monasteries. It houses one of the largest Buddhist statues, the 15 meter tall Champa, the Buddha of Future. About a hundred monks live here who follow traditional ways of running the monastery and teach monks and villagers. This Gompa is situated on the top of the hill and the 12-storey monastery complex contains numerous stupas, statues, thangkas, wall paintings, swords and a large pillar

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Handicrafts- Wood
sections.content: Today, Kashmir is also known throughout the world for its exquisite crafts which are as diverse as woolen textiles, hand-woven carpets, to the intricately designed papier-mâché, wood work, silverware, etc. Beautifully crafted objects out of walnut including superbly carved furniture items such as wall hangings, jewellery boxes, screens, room dividers, fruit bowls, trays, etc. are made by expert craftsmen. It is a wonderful combination of chiselling and carving. The exquisite lattice work on screens resembles marble lattice work done on marble.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Handicrafts- Wool
sections.content: Pashmina, Shahtoosh and Jamawar are the best known among Kashmirs superbly woven woollen shawls. The weaving and dyeing of these shawls has a lengthy process, which require great precision. Pattern drawing is transferred to a graph done by highly skilled craftsmen. Many shawls have weaving on both sides called do rukha. The colour combinations are fantastic and the woven designs are brilliantly complemented by superb embroidery.

sections.heading: Interesting Fact
sections.content: Pashmina is one of the world's rare fibers coming from the special undercoat or pashm of Central Asian mountain goats. Nomads living in the remote Himalayan mountains tend to these mountain goats.

sections.heading: Papier Mâché Artist
sections.content: The craft of Papier Mache involves the use of paper pulp for creating beautiful painted objects by craftsmen in lifelike images inspired from nature. Known locally as Kari Kamandari, Kashmirs outstanding papier mâché work has a glossy surface on which floral motifs such as the chinar leaf, iris, rose, tulips, hyacinth and arabesques are painted with great finesse and delicacy in sparkling tones. The creation of a papier-mache object has two processes - the sakhtsazi (making the object) and the naqashi (painting the surface). Papier Mache Photo Gallery

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Handicrafts- textiles
sections.content: Traditional hand knotted silk carpets in India can be found in Kashmir. The origins of these traditional silk carpets can be traced to the Mughal period. Do you know that to complete a large silk carpet takes about one year of intensive labour. The process of creating a hand knotted silk carpet is lengthy and a lot of preparation has to be made by the craftsman before weaving the carpet. The yarn used for weaving determines the type of the carpet to be created. Woolen carpets are always created on a cotton base with woolen yarn. Silk yarn is sometimes used in woolen carpets as highlights on certain designs and motifs. The most recurring motif that is found on these carpets is the tree of life. The natural beauty of Kashmir and its picturesque views have inspired the carpet weavers. Other popular themes are: hunting scenes, bird and animal motifs and historical themes. These carpets come in a variety of colors and designs. Carpets from Kashmir are unique because they are made with yarn dyed with mineral colors. Hues of red, blue and yellow color are mainly used. Two very different and interesting floor coverings are namdas and gabbas of Kashmir. They are both very attractive and distinctive in its own way. The base of namda is a locally prepared felt. Highly decorative designs are embroidered and created with appliqué work, sometimes by laying dyed wool and pressing it on the surface. The designs are mostly floral and geometrical. Gabba is a rug made from old woollens on which different coloured cut out forms are secured with chain stitch. The edges and the central portion are covered with large embroidery. They usually have bright flashes of design against a sombre background.

sections.heading: Collections of Pratap Singh Museum
sections.content: In Kashmir, Museums at Jammu and Srinagar display valuable collections of miniature paintings, sculptures and terracotta. Shri Pratap Singh Museum, Srinagar has the collections of bronze and stone sculptures of seventh to eleventh centuries of Buddhist as well as Hindu deities in the distinctive style of Kashmir.

sections.heading: Amar Mahal Palace Museum
sections.content: in Jammu is a beautiful red sand stone palace. The highlight of the museum is the splendid 120 kg golden throne, which is ornamented by the golden lions embedded into it. There is a gallery that exhibits Pahari paintings and

sections.heading: Jammu-Kashmir- Museum- Dogra Art Museum
sections.content: Dogra Art Museum has on its display about 800 rare and exquisite paintings from different schools of miniature paintings such as Basohli, Jammu and Kangra. It houses a gold plated bow and manuscripts of Shahnama and Sikandarnama, written in Persian.

sections.heading: Ruf Dance
sections.content: The Ruf Dance is a part of Kashmiri life from time immemorial. The dance has been a part of Kashmiri life from ancient times. This dance is performed to welcome the spring. In the dance, two or four groups are formed consisting of 2 to 3 women. They stand facing each other holding hands of their partner. The women together sway their feet forward and backward. The song sung in the performance is in the form of question and answer form where one group questions and the other respond to it in rhythm.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Performing Arts- Dance- Hafiza
sections.content: The Hafiza dance form is very popular. This dance form is usually performed at wedding ceremonies. Hafiz Nagma is based on the classical music of Kashmir- the Sufiyiana Kalam. The Sufiyana Kalam has its own ragas known as Muquam. The prominent instrument used in Hafiz Nagma is called Santoor-a hundred stringed instrument played with sticks. The danseuse in this tradition is known as 'Hafiza'.

sections.heading: Jammu & Kashmir- Performing Arts- Musical Instruments
sections.content: The most popular Kashmiri musical instruments are the santoor, rabab, dukra, sitar and nagara.
